1:
The occasion is argued by three of them and settled the same way by two. Keil and Delitzsch say it is hardly possible for a psalm to coincide so exactly with a known historical situation as this does with the overthrow of the Assyrian army before Jerusalem, and note the Greek title that names the Assyrian. John Calvin reports a different opinion, the deliverance from the Ammonites in a later reign, and sets it aside, preferring the Assyrians and the night in which one angel destroyed the besieging army, citing the same Greek title. Adam Clarke collects a third: the Syriac calls it a thanksgiving for the taking of a city of Ammon, while the Latin and Greek make it a psalm for the Assyrians, and the best commentators put it after the defeat of Sennacherib. Calvin and Clarke also share a doubt about the author. Both hold the psalm later than David, Clarke adding that the separation of the two kingdoms is evident from the first verse, and both conclude that either an older singer’s work was adopted or the writer was a descendant of the same name.

The first line divides them more sharply. Augustine of Hippo reports that the Jews glory in this psalm and revile the Gentiles to whom God is not known, and turns the boast round: God is indeed known nowhere but in Judah, if they understand what Judah is, since the apostle makes the Jew the one who is so in secret, in circumcision of the heart; those who glory in the name and have lost the deeds are Jews in flesh and heathens in heart. John Gill takes the same turn, referring the knowledge to those who are Jews inwardly, the true circumcision. Matthew Henry keeps it national and makes the favour the greater for being distinguishing; C.H. Spurgeon says that if he were unknown in all the world beside he is no unknown God to his people. Charles Ellicott looks at the four place-names instead, arranged by introversion, the restricted terms first and last and the general ones between, the order chosen simply for the rhythm.

At the second verse Ellicott makes the boldest proposal here. The received renderings, he says, quite obliterate the image, which is a beast of prey crouching ready for its spring, and he translates: in Salem is his covert, and his lair in Zion. Everyone else has a tabernacle. Clarke notes that Salem was the city’s ancient name and that the psalm must be later than the temple; Henry, who has God keeping court there and issuing orders by his oracles, remembers that a tabernacle is a movable dwelling and warns that the light is with us yet a little while. Keil and Delitzsch, at the mountains of prey in the next verse, keep the same predatory register, taking the phrase for haughty possessors of power who plunder all who come near.

The arrows draw fire from two directions. Clarke identifies them as the fiery kind, inflammable matter rolled round the heads and set alight, shot into towns to burn them and among the wooden works of besiegers; he gives the Roman name, quotes a line of Virgil, and reports an old commentator describing a dart with a leaden head to which fire was attached. Ellicott renders the word literally as flashes and offers three derivations: the lightning speed of an arrow’s flight, the custom of shooting bolts tipped with flame, or a connection with a word that elsewhere means pestilence. He ends by noting the fine poetic touch in the climactic use of battle to sum up all the weapons of war, which John Wesley takes as all the power of the army put in array. Spurgeon puts the verse in a sentence: without leaving his tranquil abode he sent forth his word and snapped his enemies’ arrows before they could shoot them.
4:
Who is called more glorious than the mountains of prey? John Gill reports that some take it of Zion and rejects the reading, referring it to God or to Christ and citing an old paraphrase for support. Adam Clarke takes exactly the reading Gill rejects, addressing the verse to the mountain where God dwelt and contrasting it with mountains where wild beasts prey on creatures more helpless than themselves. John Wesley agrees with Gill on the addressee and makes the mountains the greatest kings and empires, called mountains of prey because established by tyranny and maintained by preying on their own subjects or on other kingdoms. Charles Ellicott unsettles the whole verse. The construction is doubtful, the comparative of the received English is certainly to be abandoned, and the line should read that God is splendid, coming from the mountains of prey. He notes an emendation making the word fearful rather than glorious, and presses his figure from the preceding verse: the mountains are those of the Lion of Judah, until a different image suddenly interrupts, as so often in Hebrew poetry, and the hero appears from the battle shining in the spoils taken from the foe.

Ellicott then turns two more phrases inside out: the stout-hearted have let themselves be spoiled, the picture being of men rendered powerless at a glance and a word, and they have not merely slept but sunk into a deep sleep. On the men of might who did not find their hands he writes his longest note, observing that such an expression for powerlessness grew naturally into an idiom in a language that used hand for strength, quoting from another commentator in this same collection a Talmudic phrase about not finding one’s hands and feet in the school house, and comparing the Virgilian use of the word for hands and a phrase of Shakespeare about a proper fellow of my hands.

Clarke reads the sleep as suffocation, the boasting blasphemers asleep in their tents when the destroying angel, which he takes for a suffocating wind, killed the whole camp, horses and men alike in one night; and he asks whether the line about the men of might is not a strong irony, the boasted armour having vanished with them. Keil and Delitzsch keep the theology plain, that God sent forth his judiciary word from heaven into the din of war and it was immediately silenced, the earth seized with fear and its tumult obliged to cease. Ellicott finds the same word for the sleep used of the profound slumber of a defeated captain in the book of Judges, holds that two old victory songs were in the poet’s mind, and observes that they have since inspired the well-known lines of Byron on Sennacherib. Gill offers an alternative rendering, that the stout-hearted spoiled themselves, and reads the verse a second time of principalities spoiled at the cross, of the strong man disarmed in conversion, and of the destruction of antichrist.
7:
How was the judgment heard? John Gill reports that some think there was a violent clap of thunder at the moment the angel destroyed the army, thunder being the voice of God. John Wesley offers the same supposition and an alternative beside it, that the judgment is said to be heard either because it was accompanied with thunders and earthquakes or because the fame of it was quickly spread abroad. Matthew Henry states the supposition as fully as either of them — that those who date the psalm from the routing of the Assyrian army take the descent of the destroying angel to have been accompanied with thunder, and the earth’s fear to have been an earthquake soon over — and then refuses it in one sentence: this is altogether uncertain. Adam Clarke moves the hearing earlier still, to the moment when God declared by his prophet that the enemy should not prevail but should be destroyed, so that what was heard was a prophecy and not a noise.

Two of them also shrink the stage. Clarke takes the earth that feared to be the land, and by metonymy its inhabitants, struck with astonishment and terror so that they could not move, the great boaster among them struck with dumb amazement. Charles Ellicott restricts the word the same way in a gloss of four words, the meek of the land rather than of the earth, and Clarke follows him in it, making them the humbled and oppressed people of the land, now utterly helpless and calling on the Lord for succour. Henry goes the other way and takes the event as a lesson to the whole world, which is to learn from it to stand in awe of the great God.

On the stillness Henry writes the best line in the section. When God speaks judgment from heaven it is time for the earth to compose itself into an awful and reverent silence, and the silence is made, he says, as silence is made by proclamation when the court sits. He asks who may stand in God’s sight from the minute that he is angry, and answers with the figure of chaff and stubble before a consuming fire, whose anger has been kindled but a little. Keil and Delitzsch pass over the scene quickly and treat what follows as the general truth of which this deliverance is a single instance, so that the verse about the wrath of man is where the argument is really made.

The meek are defined three ways. Henry makes them the meek of the earth and the quiet in the land, those who can bear any wrong but do none, and draws out the consequence that although their meekness exposes them to injury God will sooner or later appear for their salvation and plead their cause, taking what is done against them as done against himself; the righteous God, he adds, long seems to keep silence, but sooner or later he will make judgment to be heard. Clarke, as before, keeps them local and contemporary, the poor Jews reduced to helplessness. Gill widens them in the other direction, reading the judgment heard from heaven not only of the Assyrian army but of the vials of wrath decreed against the antichristian states, and then of the last judgment itself, when the Judge shall descend, the voice of the archangel be heard, the last trumpet sound, and the dead rise from their graves to stand before the judgment seat and hear the sentence pronounced. Gill also notes, on the authority of an interpreter, that all decrees come from heaven, which is why the judgment is heard from there.
10:
Charles Ellicott begins by declaring that the text of the tenth verse as it stands is unintelligible, and takes the necessary emendation from the Greek and the Latin: not that God girds himself with the residue of wrath but that the residue of wraths does him honour, the residue meaning those who escape the enemy’s rage, which is to say the Israelites. He compares a phrase of Virgil for the remnants of a defeated host, and suggests a further rendering, that those who remain from their wrath shall keep a festival, which would carry the thought back to the escape from Egypt and the feast repeatedly demanded of Pharaoh as the purpose of that departure. Adam Clarke keeps the received text and gets the same girding out of it: as a man girds himself with his girdle that he may the better perform his work, so God will gird himself with wrath that he may destroy his enemies, pursuing the remnant of the persecutors after the first blow has fallen. He then reports how differently the Latin reads — that the thought of man shall praise God and the remains of thought keep a feast day to him — and draws a maxim from the verse: God so counterworks the evil designs of men against his cause that they turn to his glory, nor does he permit them to go the full length of what they purposed and could perform, suffering them to do some mischief but not all they would. John Wesley makes the praise come from the spectators, the furious attempts of the enemies causing God’s people and others to praise his wisdom, power and faithfulness; John Gill allows the wrath to be God’s own, with man for its object.

At the call to vow and pay, Gill turns polemical, saying that the vows meant are neither the monastic kind, which he says the Papists would infer from such words, nor ceremonial ones, but the spiritual sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving that men make in distress and ought to pay when delivered. Ellicott divides the verse between two audiences, the first clause addressed to the Israelites and the next to the heathen, and Clarke reads the second half the same way, the neighbouring nations who see the judgment bringing their homage to the terrible One lest they be consumed as the Assyrians were.

The closing verse turns on a vintage. Gill notes that the word signifies cutting as easily as a man cuts a bunch of grapes from the vine, and offers three senses of what is cut — the pride of their spirits, on the authority of an old paraphrase, or their courage, so that they flee to rocks and mountains, or their breath and life itself. Wesley says the same in a line, that God cuts them off as men do their grapes in time of vintage. Clarke leaves the figure and writes an indictment: God can fill princes with terror in the midst of their conquests or cut them off in their career of victory, and a terrible account most of them will have to give, especially those who from the lust of dominion have laid countries waste by fire and sword, making widows and orphans without number and extending the empire of desolation and death; even those whom man cannot bring to justice God will, and to judge them is one grand use of a final judgment day. Keil and Delitzsch print the two verses and add nothing.
